title: Breaking the $\sqrt{d}$ Communication Barrier in Federated Sampling with Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
claim: A single-machine sampler runs one continuous trajectory; the distributed version splits it into local runs with periodic synchronization.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, stage columns with dashed dividers on right
description: Two-panel figure. The left panel, titled Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Single Machine), shows one blue dotted trajectory spiraling from a green start circle θ0 around grey elliptical contours. Red circles mark the end of each K-step leapfrog (θ0,K, θ1,K, ..., θ(L-1),K), and a purple circle marks the final state θL,K. A legend sits underneath. The right panel, titled Distributed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, shows four colored trajectories (blue, orange, green, red) fanning out from a shared θ0 on a horizontal axis. They converge to a purple star at θ1 for synchronization, then fan out again toward θ2. Dashed vertical lines separate Stage 1 (local leapfrog), Stage 2 (communication) and Stage 3 (local leapfrog). Brace annotations read K steps, each node independently. A legend sits at the bottom. The eye goes first to the colorful trajectories.
caption: An illustration of the centralized HMC algorithm (left panel) and the federated HMC algorithm (right panel).
abstract: This work proposes the Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning (FL) tasks. The prior work on HMC applications for FL achieves $O(\sqrt{d}/Îµ)$ communication cost under log-convex distributions, already demonstrating its advantage over the Langevin dynamic-based counterpart. Based on a refined analysis, this paper further reveals the benefit of HMC for the FL regime by incorporating a control mechanism for local node shifts. We prove that AFHMC at most requires $O(\{d/Îµ^2\}^{1/3})$ communication cost up to a logarithmic term, which is significantly better than the existing results. Moreover, the proposed method adapts to client heterogeneity. Under low-heterogeneity settings (i.e., the target sampling precision $Îµ^2$ is higher than the heterogeneity level), the communication rate of AFHMC can be as good as $O(\log(d/Îµ^2))$, resembling the communication costs for FL optimization tools. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first logarithmic communication complexity result for federated sampling, even though it requires low heterogeneity. Numerically, we also justify AFHMC's advantage under the low-heterogeneity regime. Our code is available at https://github.com/laaaarrywang/Adaptive-Federated-HMC
